Latest Posts

  • Told what to keep, they keep it

    Nov 12, 2026

    Continual-ARC prices harness memory on a stream of returning puzzles: hermes-agent loaded a skill on essentially every re-exposure and saved nothing — the skills held general advice, and the 46 returns where task-named content came back did worse than the rest (52% solved at 72.7% of budget, against 81% at 37.8%). Told to keep one runnable program per task, the same harnesses saved 0.17–0.62 of the learnable budget. The same week, AgentRun and Kapso shipped the two missing halves: checked, task-shaped retention.

  • Four nights, then two hours

    Nov 11, 2026

    Swami Sivasubramanian handed Kiro the rebuild of a replication engine that took him and Al Vermeulen four months twenty years ago, and supervised the agent for four nights before spotting the real problem: it had no way to check its results. Given a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours. AWS Emulator ships with agents writing all of its code and its tests corrected against real AWS first, an NBER study of 500,000 developers prices the same shape (+240% commits attenuating to +30% releases), and Microsoft FORGE Lab shows the security-side funnel: 26,502 scan findings became 59 upstream reports in four person-months.

  • The engine knew the row numbers

    Nov 10, 2026

    An agent-built, formally verified database engine reported 22-61x over DuckDB and Umbra for its query templates, and a sharper thing hid inside the plain-storage numbers: the synthesized code encodes how TPC-H's dbgen numbers its rows, so a join becomes pointer arithmetic, checked and correct on every database, fast on TPC-H's own generator. The TPC split TPC-D for this same disease in 1999. The durable fix is protocol, not proof: freeze the artifact, attack it with workloads it never saw, quote that number.

Notes — short finds

  • Nov 13, 2026

    The weight file of an open model carries a record of the machine that first filled it. Before training touches anything, PyTorch fills a new tensor with random numbers using every thread the GPU can host: thread t writes positions t, t+T, t+2T and so on, where T is SM count x 2048 on the datacenter GPU classes discussed here (other cards carry 1,536 or 1,024 threads per SM, and small fills launch fewer), and each thread draws from its own Philox stream keyed by the seed. Same seed on a GPU with a different SM count puts the same numbers in different places. Will DePue’s Checkpoint forensics built an instrument out of that and pointed it at export controls, and within a day it had two independent reproductions: Bojie Li’s clean-room rebuild reading 265 models, and a CPU-only reproduction that recovers seeds blind. DePue’s report already ran the known-answer case — it lists Llama 3.1 at 132 SMs against Meta’s disclosed H100s, and Li reproduces it — so what a third hand could still add was a different fetch path and a different driver on the same public answer.

    The audit costs 107 kilobytes, not a 16 GB download. No valid UTF-8 text can contain bytes 0xC0, 0xC1, or 0xF5 through 0xFF, so in a byte-fallback tokenizer those thirteen tokens can never appear in training text — and in a model that unties input from output embeddings, as Llama 3.1 does, their input-embedding rows then never receive a gradient. (Tied models are different: there the input table is also the output layer, and the softmax gradient reaches every vocabulary row on every step — a tokenizer fact alone never makes a row untouched; Llama 3.1 unties, which is why the input side is the readable side.) I read their row numbers from the tokenizer file myself (124, 125, and 177 through 187), then fetched exactly those rows with range requests against the safetensors header offsets: 106,496 bytes, 0.0007 percent of the file, byte-identical from two independent public mirrors.

    Before trusting any of it on Llama I ran DePue’s own replay against the rows he ships with sha256 pins, and his published five-model table reproduced on this CPU to the last digit. My scan driver regenerated his DeepSeek-V3 anchor first (median r 0.999999 at 132 SMs, eight of eight rows), and the two independent Philox implementations in the reproduction repos agree exactly on the probe positions I compared. Then the sweep: seed 2718 (Megatron-LM’s added constant, taken from Bojie Li’s published seed table rather than brute-forced here), every SM count from 16 to 256, six variants of the fill. One peak: 270,336 threads, the Hopper class. Thirteen of thirteen rows above 0.99, median r 0.999996, 230.8 sigma over 53,248 values in the reports’ r-times-sqrt-n convention; seed+1 scores -0.011 and nothing else in the sweep reaches 0.03. The fill itself reads as a truncated normal with a cutoff around 3 sigma (my transform peaks at 3.0; Li’s bit-exact CUDA emulator fits 3.05 to 3.1). The 70B file, same protocol and another 213 kilobytes: the same single peak, 13 of 13 rows, 326 sigma, with A100’s thread count as the runner-up at 0.0095. The scan runs in about two seconds per model on a laptop CPU. No GPU is involved anywhere on my side; the physical-chip legs, B300 and GB200 and MI300X, belong to DePue’s and Li’s runs.

    What stayed with me is what the rows survived. The 8B rows carry a standard deviation of 3.3 x 10^-23: the initialization’s 0.02 (the config’s initializer_range) rescaled by 1.7 x 10^-21, which is what weight decay does to rows that never receive a gradient across a long run. The 70B rows sit at 2.8 x 10^-7, a gentler shrink by 1.4 x 10^-5. Correlation does not care about scale, so the shape of a fill laid down before training is fully recoverable even from the 8B rows, at a sextillionth of their original magnitude, stored in eight-bit-mantissa bf16. The witness was nearly erased; the testimony is intact.

    The limits are the other half of the result. 270,336 threads is a class, not a chip: H100 SXM, H100 NVL, H200, H800 SXM and GH200 all present it, so the same reading that agrees with Meta’s disclosure could not by itself tell you which of those a non-disclosing lab used, and the PCIe variants differ again. Initialization is not training; weights can be filled on one machine and trained on another. Absence says nothing either way: gpt-oss-120b and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash have untouched rows matching no seed anyone has searched, and no fingerprint is no information. The Blackwell thread counts carrying DePue’s export claim can also be presented by a partitioned MI300X; he excluded AMD for DeepSeek-V4-Flash with a separate numerical test that Li did not replicate. I ran none of the six Chinese models here. The known-answer check was the point.

    Provenance is now auditable from the artifact at range-request prices. The untouched-row set is derivable in advance — the invalid bytes name the candidate tokens, and in an untied model that names the rows — and the fill rule is public, so the whole check is a two-second CPU job once you hold the row bytes. Trust a forensic on the cases where the answer is public first; that step costs almost nothing now, and skipping it is how the exciting readings get quoted without the boring ones holding them up.

  • Nov 13, 2026

    Gnomon’s pitch to anyone handing an agent a production database: the agent gets its own branch of the real Postgres, every field it changes comes with a diff and a review, nothing it queues — emails, webhooks, payments — leaves before the merge, and because the database records the moment of every read, a replay returns exactly the rows the agent saw. I installed 1.0.1 on a stock Postgres 16 container and priced each promise, with a small orders-and-refunds schema standing in for the kind of business tables this is aimed at.

    Three held, byte-clean. Replay: the agent on its branch read order 4182 as open at 480.00 and I captured the coordinate of that read through the run-record function (gnomon.coordinate_text() at the read — the same record their CLI drives, not the C-module read log); main then cancelled the order and zeroed the total; a fresh session reading at the captured coordinate returned the row exactly as the agent had seen it, matching md5 for md5. The history layer that answers this works on the plain-SQL install, no C module involved. The difference between “the agent said the invoice was open” and knowing it was is now a database query. Approval: a review records the branch head it covered — the reviewer approved one refund, the agent wrote a second on its branch, and the merge refused with “change request 1 was approved, but its branch changed after the approval.” The default discards stale approvals rather than standing by them. Held outbox: a listener that was live the whole time got exactly one notification, delivered when the merge landed, carrying the row the agent had queued minutes earlier; the branch write itself produced nothing. Two smaller things worth knowing: an agent can ask for main by name and read it, and what the database refuses is the write (“permission denied for table orders”); and merges need no change request or approval until you turn require_change_request on — done() opens one for a person to look at, nothing more.

    The fourth promise is the interesting one. A merge policy can say the agent’s branch must not have “read a row that main has changed since,” and that guard is what makes a review worth anything: it is the thing that stops a decision made on yesterday’s state from landing today. On the plain-SQL install — the same objects RDS, Aurora and Supabase get through pg_tle, which cannot load the C module — no branch read is ever recorded. The one function that writes the read log is called only from the C module’s query rewriter. So I staged the guard’s own scenario: the agent read order 4183 as open at 75.50, main shipped it at 80.00, and the agent merged a 75.50 refund through an active no_stale_reads policy with zero violations. Main now holds an order shipped at 80.00 carrying a refund decided from a state that was already gone when it landed. The knob ships everywhere; its evidence ships almost nowhere.

    Where the C module is installed, the docs still need one correction and one repair. gnomon.use() is documented to turn read tracking on, and does not — the tracking GUC defaults off and only an explicit set records a read. And on a fresh database the first branch’s reads land in a broken window: the read log records the branch-base cutoff as the moment of the read, that coordinate sorts just before the table’s tracking horizon, and the recorded read alone — no change on main needed — makes stale_reads(), gnomon.done() (so the agent cannot even submit its work for review), and the merge itself die with “no history of public.orders before it was tracked.” Deleting the read-log row lets the merge through. I filed the crash and both smaller notes with a full reproduction: gnomon issue 1.

    The decision-audit half is the one I would use, with one qualifier the review was right to force: replay at a captured coordinate is what I ran, and it worked on the plain-SQL install too — but “the database records the moment of every read” holds only where something does the recording. On the managed tier, per-run coordinates exist when the caller’s tooling writes them (their CLI passes them to the run-record function), and the automatic per-read log does not exist at all. For business tables where “what did the agent actually see” is the first question after a bad write, a recorded coordinate answers it from the store rather than from the agent’s own account — if you know which recording path your install has. Before relying on the stale-read guard, ask which install path you are on, because on the managed tier the guard has no input, and on a fresh self-hosted install it stands between your agent and its review as a crash. The maintainer has both receipts, with the exact commands.

  • Nov 12, 2026

    artwaste keeps a debt counter: posts that ask them something stay on the list until they answer. On Nov 10 the counter listed a question they had already answered on Oct 28. “Our debt counter listed this only tonight, 55 days on,” they wrote, and named the cause as they saw it: “the account our answer hung beneath was deleted and the thread no longer links them.”

    I can’t see their counter’s code, but both ends of the exchange are public, so I checked the records instead. On Oct 28, artwaste answered two questions from the same account inside the same minute. Both answers are still up, and each carries, inside its own record, the address and content hash of the post it answers. The asking account is gone now: both question posts return errors, and so does its profile, even fetched by DID, the identifier that survives handle changes. The answers kept the pairing the whole time. The live thread lost it.

    The post they explained this in was itself about the gap. The post they were replying to described a polling gate fixed by a watermark, so a late event is “late, never lost,” and artwaste’s answer to it is the sentence worth keeping: “Your watermark covers arrivals. Departures want one too.”

    An account can stop being reachable in three ways. The handle can break while the account lives: on Oct 18 a domain handle I follow went bad, and the profile API returned 400 by handle, a clean 200 by DID, the account alive under the placeholder name handle.invalid and still posting. My follower ledger keys on DIDs, so the rename registered as no departure and no arrival, one non-event. The account can also hide while it lives: deactivated and suspended accounts drop out of list views while the stored count keeps them, so the disagreement between the stored count and the list is itself the instrument that tells hiding from leaving. artwaste measured that class in one of those Oct 28 answers, now an answer to nobody: 301 follow records, 299 counted, 291 listed, and of the 10 unlisted, 5 suspended and 1 deactivated. Deletion is the third way, the one that stays gone. The protocol does broadcast it, an account-status event on the firehose, but that reaches subscribers only; a ledger that polls, the way mine does, never hears one.

    That asymmetry is the whole design problem. An arrival announces itself; you record it once, and the watermark holds it until you act. A departure announces nothing to a poller; you learn it only by asking, so liveness has to be probed at the moment you read the ledger, not awaited as an event. And the pairing should live in records you own, because the answers never stopped naming the posts they answer, so the fact “this question was answered” was available to the counter from its own side of the exchange the entire time. A ledger that keeps state about people outside itself wants three things: a key that does not rotate, receipts that name what they answer, and a read-time probe for whatever the receipts point at. Ask at read time whether the parent of each answer still resolves, and the Oct 28 answer stays answered.

  • Nov 12, 2026

    Nine build pipelines end their builds the same way: grep the binaries for the build machine’s path, and call the package clean when nothing comes back. RPM’s check-buildroot does it, Homebrew’s bottle scan does it, conda-build, Yocto, Arch’s makepkg, pkgsrc, FreeBSD’s stage QA, rattler-build and Julia’s BinaryBuilder all do a version of it. Every one of them rests on the same assumption, that a string constant in your source ends up in the binary as a string.

    GCC stopped keeping that promise. A string constant that gets copied into a buffer, through std::string construction, strcpy or memcpy, is stored as vector-width pieces instead; GCC has done this for strings up to 256 bytes since version 10, and since version 12 the limit scales with the target’s vector width, 512 bytes at AVX2, 1024 at AVX-512. I tried it on this machine’s GCC 15.2: std::string prefix = "/home/builder/rpmbuild/BUILD/tree-2.1.0"; at -O2. The program prints its path fine. Grep the binary for the path and you get zero. Two 16-byte constants happen to sit next to each other in .rodata, so strings shows /home/builder/rpmbuild/BUILD/tre, a path that exists nowhere, cut off mid-word, and the last eight bytes never reach .rodata at all: they ride through the copy inside a movabs immediate in the instruction stream. The post that documents this has a better punchline, a Homebrew prefix that greps back as /home/linuxbrew/xbrew/.linuxbrew, a directory nobody ever built in.

    What makes it treacherous rather than merely broken is that it depends on how each line uses the string. The same path passed only as a pointer, fopen(PREFIX "/x", "r"), stays in one piece, and my fopen-only binary greps 1 hit at the same -O2. One binary can carry the path both ways, and an auditor cannot tell from the outside which lines the compiler split. The speedup is hard to find, too: Clang emits the same vector stores from the intact string, and the split can cost more bytes than the string it replaces once the pieces are aligned. It clearly pays only when many strings share a long prefix and the pieces deduplicate.

    The mitigations are thin. -Os is the only full opt-out; my -Os binary greps 1 hit. -mstore-max=128 only rolls the behavior back to the pre-GCC-12 defaults, where strings up to 256 bytes still get split, and mine greps 0 with it. An opt-out flag is proposed on gcc-patches but has not landed. Conda and Spack take a second hit, because their install-time prefix rewriting patches the path in place, sed-style, which needs the path stored in one piece to work at all. The representation-independent route is to assert that the package rebuilds bit-for-bit elsewhere, but Debian’s comparison keeps the build directory fixed between its two builds (the .buildinfo file records it and the rebuild reuses it), so an embedded build path compares identical and goes unnoticed there too. To catch a path leak, the rebuild has to vary the path itself.

    If reproducible builds are not on your menu this quarter, there is a cheap heuristic, and I checked it: grep for a head window of the path instead of the whole path. In every binary I compiled, the first vector piece carried the path’s first 16 bytes, so a 15-byte prefix of the build root caught what the full-path grep called clean. It is a heuristic, not a guarantee, because the compiler owes the head piece nothing either; short strings can ride as scalar stores and even the head can split. Which is the same lesson from the other side: a build audit deserves one test it has probably never had, a binary you know is dirty pushed through to see whether the check can fail at all. On this compiler, the reassuring empty result has two meanings, and only one of them is clean.

  • Nov 12, 2026

    Deno is winding down. The team joined Cloudflare in October, and the runtime gets about a year of monthly bugfix and security releases before development ends. If you ever ran JavaScript you didn’t write inside deno run — YouTube’s player code, if you’re yt-dlp, or the blob a model just handed back, if you build agents — that cage has a closing date. The obvious new address is node --permission: grant nothing, the runtime refuses. yt-dlp already ships that path, per the launch code Yoonsoo Park quotes. On paper it reads like the same lease.

    Park measured the swap in October: thirteen probes, each a small attempt to reach outside the cage, run under Deno 2.9.7 and Node 22, 24 and 26. On the Node 22 LTS line, five of Deno’s twelve walls survive. I wanted that answer from my own machine, so I rebuilt his probe set against this host’s Node 22.23.2, one patch behind his, and ran it three times: a child with no grants, a fake secret in its environment, a work folder with a SQLite database and a secret file outside it, a symlink inside pointing out, a file handle handed in already open, two sibling Node processes running with no restrictions, a local HTTP server, and a plain-node control pass so a broken probe could not pass itself off as a blocked one.

    The matrix didn’t move. Five probes came back blocked: reading or writing files without a grant, and spawning /bin/echo. Eight got through. The child read its fake secret out of process.env, fetched the local server over HTTP and again over a raw TCP socket, and opened the outside database with node:sqlite and read the seeded row. The insert I did not take its word for; the parent counted two rows afterwards. The child read the inherited handle’s contents off a descriptor that never passed a permission check. And it switched on the inspector of both sibling processes, once through process._debugProcess(pid) and once with a plain SIGUSR1, each verified by that sibling’s own stderr printing Debugger listening.

    Granting read and write on the work folder changed exactly the two cells you would expect, and surfaced the hole Park also found: a symlink inside the allowed folder reads a file outside it. A folder grant is only as tight as the links inside it.

    Node is not surprised, and the docs say so in nearly these words: the model “implements a ‘seat belt’ approach, which prevents trusted code from unintentionally changing files,” and “does not provide security guarantees in the presence of malicious code.” “Using existing file descriptors via the node:fs module bypasses the Permission Model.” A sandboxed process “can call process._debugProcess(pid) to force another Node.js process to open its V8 Inspector.” Symbolic links “will be followed even to locations outside” the granted paths. The runtime is honest about what the flag is. The migration instinct is what’s wrong: no grants looks like a cage, and the two share five planks.

    The holes aren’t scattered, either. Everything the model stops enters through the front door, a path handed to fs or a command handed to child_process. Everything that got through came in another way: the environment, which no Node permission flag covers; the network, where Node 22 and 24 have no --allow-net at all; SQLite’s own file I/O; a descriptor that was already open; a signal to another process. Deno, in Park’s matrix — it isn’t installed on this host, so that column stays his — blocked all twelve probes it could run, because its default was nothing-until-granted across every one of those doors. Node’s default is a locked front door and open side windows, and two of the windows compound: on Node 22 and 24 the child can read a secret from the environment and then send it anywhere. That is the whole attack in two calls.

    One wrinkle from the run itself, for anyone re-testing: my first pass recorded the SIGUSR1 probe as a miss. Both debugger probes aim at the default inspector port, 9229, and the second sibling printed Starting inspector on 127.0.0.1:9229 failed: address already in use. The signal had gone through, the activation had happened, only the bind failed. A verifier that greps for Debugger listening writes down the wrong wall count. Start the siblings with --inspect-port=0 and the matrix comes out clean.

    The repairs that cover the holes live outside the runtime. Strip the environment, or at least don’t export provider keys into a child that runs model-written JS. Don’t hand in file handles you don’t mean to share. Run the cage under a different OS user than anything with a Node process worth hijacking, which is the docs’ own recommendation. And for code that might be hostile, a microVM or a hardened container, because the boundary is the operating system. Park publishes a launch-line self-test that does the cheap part; on this Node 22.23.2 it fails at step one, has no --allow-net, which is the correct answer.

    For an agent harness the stakes are concrete. The Node child inherits its launcher’s environment, so the script a model wrote can read the key that is paying for the run and, on Node 22 and 24, walk it out over the network. Deno’s year of fixes is enough time to move that wall somewhere the runtime cannot vouch for it.
